clues.title: Driving side: left
text: Malta drives on the **left**.
NOTE: Cyprus also drives on the left.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Cars drive on the left. Cyprus also drives on the left, so this narrows it to Malta or Cyprus.

clues.title: Plate: EU blue strip, often short
text: Like most of Europe, Maltese licence plates have a blue strip on the left. However, unlike most of Europe, **short plates** are very common.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Plates have the blue strip on the left like most of Europe, but short, almost square plates are very common here.

clues.title: Landscape: dry fields, cacti, narrow roads
text: The general landscape of Malta consists of slightly hilly **dry agricultural fields**. Many roads are also only 1 or 2 lanes wide, due to the island’s size. Having a mediterranean climate, [cacti](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Kh2pMFPUTQhivKT76#extra%5Btags%5D=yes) and various [dry shrubs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/BqgdrBxdG2UFft3z7#extra%5Btags%5D=yes) can be seen.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Gently hilly, dry farm fields with cacti and dry shrubs. Many roads are only one or two lanes wide because the island is small.

clues.title: Walls: pale limestone rock walls
text: **Limestone rock walls** are extremely common in Malta. This alone is usually enough to determine that you are in Malta.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Low walls made of stacked pale limestone rock line the fields and roads. This alone is usually enough to tell you it is Malta.

clues.title: Houses: low, white to beige walls
text: The vast majority of buildings in Malta consist of low storey buildings, with **white to beige** coloured walls. Buildings made of [limestone](https://maps.app.goo.gl/BMSfQdQ7rujtEErg8#extra%5Btags%5D=yes) are also fairly common.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most buildings are low, with white to beige walls. Limestone-built houses are also fairly common.

clues.title: Houses: covered wooden balconies
text: This style of traditional **covered balconies** is very common on Maltese buildings. They are often painted in bright colours.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Traditional enclosed balconies stick out from the walls of many buildings. They are often painted in bright colours.

clues.title: Sign: street name with "triq"
text: The Maltese word for street is “**triq**”, which can be seen on almost every street sign.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The word "triq" means street and appears on almost every street name sign.

clues.title: Bus stops: common, with local info
text: **Bus stops** are a common sight in Malta. They may sometimes have useful information as to where you are.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bus stops are everywhere on the islands. They sometimes show useful information, like route numbers or place names, that tells you where you are.

clues.title: Road lines: double yellow no-parking lines
text: Like the UK and Ireland, Malta uses these distinctive **double yellow no parking lines**.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Two yellow lines along the kerb mean no parking, as in the UK and Ireland. With left-hand driving, that narrows it to those countries or Malta.

clues.title: Language: English is everywhere
text: **English** is the primary language of Malta.

images.caption: Car dealer window sign in English: import vehicles directly from the UK

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: English is the main language, so you will see lots of English signs and shop names.

clues.title: Language: Maltese letters Ċ Ġ Ħ Ż
text: Apart from English it is also common to see the **Maltese** language. Maltese uses the Latin script, but with unique letters, which include:
- Ċ ċ
- Ġ ġ
- Ħ ħ
- Ż ż

images.caption: Maltese text with the letters Ċ Ġ Ħ Ż shown large

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Maltese uses Latin letters plus special ones with dots or bars: Ċ, Ġ, Ħ and Ż. It is related to Arabic but has many Italian words.

clues.title: Guardrail: low stone barriers instead
text: Regular metal guardrails are rare on Gozo Island. **Low stone barriers** are more common instead.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: On the small island of Gozo, normal metal guardrails are rare. Low stone barriers line the roads instead.

clues.title: Bus routes: numbers in the 300s
text: Uniquely, all bus routes on Gozo Island are in the **300s**. These can be quite hard to see, meaning they are most useful in moving games.

images.caption: Red box marks the route number 310 on the lower part of the bus stop sign

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Every bus route on Gozo has a number in the 300s. They are hard to spot, so they mostly help in games where you can move.

clues.title: Sign: blue signs unique to the capital
text: These **blue signs** are unique to Valletta.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: These blue signs are only found in the capital, Valletta, so seeing one tells you where on the island you are.

clues.title: Coverage: backpack shots on a white-blue ferry
text: This trekker on a ship that is painted **white and blue** can be seen between the main island and Gozo Island.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The coverage taken on a white and blue ship crosses between the main island and Gozo.
